newsitem.title: USA: Dow Corning asks decision on implant-disease issue.
newsitem.headline: Dow Corning asks decision on implant-disease issue.

text.p: Dow Corning Corp., in a bid to advance its bankruptcy reorganization plan, Monday asked a judge to decide once and for all the controversial issue of whether silicone-gel breast implants cause disease.

Dow Corning said it filed a motion in U.S. Bankruptcy Court in Bay City, Mich., objecting to claims that its implants are to blame for a variety of diseases in women, such as lupus and other autoimmune disorders.
For the first time, Dow Corning is formally seeking to separate such disease claims from those involving implant ruptures and local complications, which it is more willing to consider paying.
The motion asks U.S. Bankruptcy Judge Arthur Spector to make a summary judgment as to whether scientific evidence justifies claims that silicone implants cause disease.

If he rules in Dow Corning's favour, the silicone products company could avoid paying about $1.4 billion earmarked for resolution of disease claims as part of its proposed plan of reorganization. Dow has earmarked only $600 million to pay claims for ruptures and local complications, or problems that occur in the breast tissue surrounding the implant.

Dow Corning, a 54-year-old joint venture between Dow Chemical Co. and Corning Inc., was once the nation's largest maker of silicone-gel breast implants. It was pushed into bankruptcy court nearly two years ago by a crush of litigation over health claims.

The bankruptcy proceedings froze all lawsuits against the company, forcing hundreds of thousands of women to wait until the company's reorganization plan is approved before their claims can be resolved.

At present, the bankruptcy court, located about 20 miles from Dow Corning's headquarters in Midland, Mich., has received about 500,000 implant-related claims. It is unclear how many women are involved in the claims.

Dow Corning has long maintained that scientific studies prove that breast implants pose no increased risk of disease. It said its motions parallel several recent court decisions in which judges have allowed claims on ruptures and local complications involving other manufacturers to move forward to trial, but have found evidence insufficient to support claims that silicone implants cause disease.

"We're trying to move this along toward a fair and prompt resolution," Dow Corning Chairman Richard Hazleton said. "If we get the disease cauasation issue resolved, we can get on with resolving the local complications claims."
He said Dow Corning is willing to compensate women with ruptures and local complications "on a reasonable basis, where appropriate."
The motions were filed as the bankruptcy court is preparing for an April 16 hearing on whether breast implant plaintiffs should be allowed to file an alternate plan of reorganization for Dow Corning.
Plaintiff lawyers, unhappy with Dow Corning's proposed $600 million local complications fund, want to submit their own plan, but have not disclosed details.

"I believe the filing of these motions on the eve of the exclusivity hearing is a desperate attempt to avoid an adverse decision on exclusivity," said Edward Blizzard, a Houston attorney who is representing tort clamaints in the bankruptcy case.
Nonetheless, he said plantiff attorneys are confident that any ruling by Spector will show that implants cause disease, allowing lawyers to concentrate on the task of valuing those claims.
Hazleton said Dow Corning also is confident that Spector will rule in its favour and is "willing to live with the outcome."

Dow Corning also has proposed that Spector, in making the decision, use the expertise of a national scientific panel established last year by U.S. District Judge Sam Pointer in Birmingham, Ala. Pointer is handling litigation involving other breast implant manufacturers who have reached a separate, open-ended settlement with plaintiffs.
